history.idea: Replace random order with a target-similarity filter: (1) drop exact/near duplicates (hash of whitespace-normalised lowercase first 500 chars) and obvious junk (docs under 200 chars, non-ASCII-letter ratio high, or fraction of words found in the target_sample vocabulary < 0.5, which catches scrambled-letter text and code). (2) Train a classifier: TfidfVectorizer(analyzer='char_wb', ngram_range=(2,4), max_features=200k, sublinear_tf=True) on the first 3000 chars of each text, LogisticRegression(C=10) with positives = the 200 target_sample docs (class_weight='balanced') and negatives = a seeded random 4000 pool docs; score all surviving pool docs. Also add a hard bonus for WikiText formatting cues (doc starts with '= ' title line, contains ' @-@ ', ' , ', ' . ' tokenised punctuation). (3) Rank by score, take the top docs until their gpt2 token count (estimate via tiktoken on docs, or len(chars)/4 if time is tight) reaches about 1.0*T; if the clearly-target-like set (score above the midpoint between the mean target-sample cross-validated score and the mean pool score) holds less than T tokens, still fill up to T with the next best-scoring docs rather than cycling unless the target-like set is at least 0.5*T, in which case return only that set (it will be cycled). (4) Shuffle the selected indices with the CURATE_SEED-seeded RNG and return.
history.outcome: dev 1.9206 against 1.9408 for the best at the time, KEPT as the new best

history.idea: Add a word-order / damage quality filter and stronger dedup on top of the current pipeline, and never fill with junk. (1) Word-order filter: build a set of lowercase word bigrams (whitespace tokens) from the 200 target_sample docs. For each surviving pool doc, compute over its first 6000 chars (a) bigram coverage = fraction of its adjacent word pairs found in the target bigram set, (b) function-word plausibility = fraction of occurrences of ' the ' followed by a token that is not in {',', '.', 'the', 'of', 'and'}, and (c) fraction of whitespace tokens that are in the target vocabulary. Calibrate thresholds from the target itself: split target_sample in two halves, build bigrams from one half, measure (a)/(b)/(c) on the other half, scale (a) for the half-size set by also measuring pool docs with the same half set, and drop pool docs falling below the 2nd-percentile target value minus a small margin on any of the three. This catches word-shuffled, sentence-spliced and character-corrupted Wikipedia-like docs that the char_wb classifier cannot see. (2) Stronger dedup: besides the first-500-char hash, also dedup on the normalised title line ('= Title =') and on hashes of three 200-char windows taken at 25%, 50% and 75% of the doc; when duplicates collide keep the one with the highest bigram coverage, then the longest. (3) Selection: rank the remaining docs by classifier score + format bonus as now, but only fill up to T with docs above the target-like threshold; if that clean set holds at least 0.3*T tokens return just it (cycled) rather than padding with lower-scoring off-domain docs; otherwise pad as before. Keep the seeded shuffle.
history.outcome: dev 1.8142 against 1.9206 for the best at the time, KEPT as the new best

history.idea: Replace the LogisticRegression classifier with a simpler but faster and often more robust 'TF-IDF Cosine Similarity' approach. Compute the average TF-IDF vector of the 200 target_sample docs (using char_wb, n-gram (2,4), 200k features) and score pool docs by their cosine similarity to this centroid. This avoids the training overhead and potential overfitting/instability of a small LogisticRegression model on a noisy, small target set.

Replace the LogisticRegression classifier with a TF-IDF Cosine Similarity model: compute the centroid vector of the target_sample using TfidfVectorizer(analyzer='char_wb', ngram_range=(2,4), max_features=200000, sublinear_tf=True), then score all pool docs by their cosine similarity to this centroid.

Introduce a 'high-density' weighting to the final score: for each document, calculate the 'information density' as the ratio of (total characters - whitespace characters) / (number of unique words). Multiply the final classifier score by this density, capped at a factor of 2.0. This prioritizes docs with rich, varied vocabulary over repetitive or highly redundant texts that the classifier might still rank highly.
